title: How AI uses your Gmail for ads (explained simply)
description: How AI uses your Gmail for ads changed on October 16, 2026, when Google's privacy policy added a conditional exception for linked services. This video explains the default protection, the one optional choice that lets a Gmail request feed an AI feature like Gemini's Personal Intelligence, and how that context can later influence ads. It separates what Google's systems can process from what an advertiser ever receives, corrects the two common scare stories, and shows which settings limit future use without erasing data already saved. It ends with one simple decision rule and flags the details most likely to change.

scenes.say: You asked Gemini to find one email — your exam hall ticket. Simple and helpful. But did that same request help decide which ads you see?
By the end you'll know exactly what changed in Google's privacy policy on October 16, 2026, who really sees your data, and the settings worth checking tonight.
I'm Thoma, your friendly neighbourhood tech imp. Let's poke at this policy carefully, because the scary version going around leaves out one small condition.
Start with the rule that didn't change. Google says the content of your Gmail, Drive and Photos is not used for personalized ads by default.
Personalized ads just means ads picked from signals about you, things like what you search or watch, not only from the page in front of you.
Now the exception. Data from a linked service — an app you've connected to Google, like Gmail — can inform ads when you share it with another Google service that supports personalized ads.

items.text: Share it with a Google service

scenes.say: Think of a school library app. You link your borrowing history to get book recommendations, and now the app knows you love mystery novels.
That taste profile can later decide which book-fair poster you see, even though the publisher never gets your library card or your reading notes.
The Google version of that assistant has a name: Personal Intelligence. It arrived in Gemini in January 2026, and it's still a beta for eligible users eighteen and over.
Beta just means it's still being tested. And the feature answers you using your linked services, drawing on personal context you chose to share.

messages.text: Here it is: 12 May, 9 a.m., hall B.

scenes.say: Here's the thread we'll follow. You turn the feature on, connect Gmail, then ask for one thing: your hall ticket. You can also skip the connection entirely.
It reads through the permitted data to answer the request. That's a program doing the reading — nobody sits there scrolling your mail just to pick ads. <laugh>

visual.sub: no one scrolls your mail just for ads

scenes.say: Now the quiet part. If that second service, the one doing the reading, supports personalized ads, that data — or the context built from it — can influence which ad you get.
Derived context just means the note the system keeps about that email — not the email itself. Something like 'exam hall ticket, 12 May, hall B'.
So who sees what? You connected the inbox. Google's AI processes it. Google's ad system may use the context. The advertiser only buys the ad space.
Advertisers don't get your messages, files or photos, and Google says it doesn't pass identifying details like your name or email address through this process.
If step-by-step breakdowns help, a new one lands every day.
Google says some categories are off-limits for targeting — choosing who sees an ad. Health, religion, race and sexual orientation are on it.
Which brings us to the picture most people have, and it's wrong. Google has not quietly switched on inbox reading for ads for everyone.
The second wrong picture is an advertiser browsing your mail like a nosy neighbour. The sources are clear that isn't what happens.
And using data inside Google to choose an ad is not the same as selling that data. Those are separate acts, even when both feel uncomfortable.
So the real trade-off isn't a scary policy page. It's a helpful request. Ask for your hall ticket, and that context may shape ads later.
You get less searching now. In exchange, that context may follow you into ad selection. You don't have to like it, but you should see it clearly.
So check the levers. Disconnect linked services from Personal Intelligence in your Google Account, and review personalized recommendations in your Search settings.
Ad preferences sit in My Ad Center. Menu names move around, so look for those words instead of memorising a path that may change.

visual.text: Ad preferences live in *My Ad Center*
visual.sub: names move; look for the words

scenes.say: Here's the catch. Disconnecting stops future access, but reporting says old data may stay in your Search services history — the record under your personalization settings.
Availability is a separate question from policy. The policy applies worldwide, but reports say the beta hasn't reached the UK, Switzerland, Nigeria or the European Economic Area yet.
Meanwhile, ChatGPT began showing labelled ads in January 2026 and later expanded to dozens of countries. Different company, different rules, same question for you.
One more honest limit: the AI writing your answer and the system picking your ads aren't necessarily the same program. The policy point is the data connection.
So back to your hall ticket. That one request can let your exam context influence ads in principle. It isn't proof that a specific ad came from your mail.
Key takeaway: convenience can turn your inbox into an ad signal, so check what's connected. Stay curious. Thoma out!
